implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM monitor through AnyRef: synchronized is a method on every reference type (used as lock.synchronized { ... } or this.synchronized), and wait/notify/notifyAll come from java.lang.Object, so a guarded Scala class is a monitor object exactly as in Java, including the single wait set and the mandatory predicate loop. Idiomatic Scala nevertheless treats shared mutable state as the exception: the futures documentation calls blocking the escape hatch, warns that blocking calls starve ExecutionContext.global unless wrapped in scala.concurrent.blocking, and pushes immutability, message passing and java.util.concurrent instead. The monitor remains the right tool when a synchronous mutable object really is shared across threads; when it is not, confinement to one ExecutionContext or an actor removes the need for it.
pitfalls: Scala closures make it easy to publish mutable state: synchronized protects only the accesses that go through the same monitor, so every escape route (returned collections, captured references, callbacks) must be guarded.

The mechanism is JVM-specific: code written this way cannot be reused on Scala.js or Scala Native, whose concurrency models differ, and blocking inside a Future or an actor thread starves the underlying pool.
Reentrancy is per JVM monitor, so calling into another synchronized Scala object while holding one monitor reproduces the nested monitor lockout hazard of Java.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent ReentrantLock + Condition
variants.implementation_notes: Where the intrinsic monitor is too limited, Scala code uses the j.u.c classes directly, exactly as Java does: ReentrantLock is the monitor lock (tryLock with timeouts, lockInterruptibly, optional fairness) and Condition instances are the wait sets, one per predicate, so a state change signals only the waiters it helps. The lock must be released in a finally block, Condition.await must run while holding the lock, and this is the usual choice inside services where blocking is unavoidable but must be bounded by timeouts or cancellable.
pitfalls: await must be inside the lock and the predicate loop remains mandatory; signalling a condition obtained from a different lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException.
Fairness defaults to off and can starve writers under contention, while fair mode costs throughput; a timed await also needs the caller to decide what a timeout means for the object's invariant.
Mixing j.u.c locks with synchronized blocks on the same object creates two independent locks, so neither serialises the whole object.
